Mr. Speaker, on Monday and Tuesday of this week the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked a series of questions in connection with the lay-off of some 900-odd workers at McKinnon Industries Limited in St. Catharines. Among the questions asked by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam were whether the union concerned had been able to secure the names of those certified by the adjustment assistance board and whether the board would be arranging a meeting with the union.
The facts are that the union applied to the board some time ago for certification of certain workers laid off at McKinnon Industries.
February 23, 1967

Inquiries of the Ministry Following an investigation the board found that there were a variety of reasons for the lay-offs, but that, in their opinion, out of the total of 900 or more who were laid off, some 395 jobs had been affected as a result of the operation of the automotive agreement.
On Monday of this week the union sent me a telegram, the one referred to in the questions by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, drawing attention to the fact that of the 900 or so workers who had been laid off, 255 male workers who had been certified by the adjustment assistance board had already returned to work. The union found this rather confusing.
As I stated in the house on Tuesday, I immediately informed the board of the contents of the telegram and I asked for a report. The board met on Tuesday of this week, and since that meeting, my information is that in determining the number of workers laid off in this dispute the board had named the 395 employees who had the most seniority at the time of what is sometimes called the "bumping process" which had been proceeded with in September of last year but which had not been completed. I pointed out that this situation does not prevail in other western democratic countries such as France and Germany, which have imported labour in substantial numbers from behind the iron curtain who have made a very large economic contribution to the prosperity of those countries. Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the minister's remarks. As he has said, the committee on industry, research and energy development spent a considerable time on this bill. Although I am a member of that committee I was unfortunately unable to attend the meetings because I am chairman of another committee. There are one or two questions which I should like to ask at this time.
The first is: If a United States subsidiary operating in Canada is given a grant under this legislation is there anything in the bill which would prevent such subsidiary using the money to develop a product which could be made by the head office of the company in the United States and sold in the United States or possibly in some other country? I want to be assured that Canada does not propose to subsidize research by a subsidiary of a United States company with the parent company then proceeding to manufacture the product of that research in the United States. I believe we should insist, if possible, that in cases in which we make a grant for the development of a product that product will be manufactured here in Canada.
I realize we are dealing with a complicated bill and that many of its clauses deal with difficult questions. One of the major problems lies in reaching a good definition of what actually constitutes research. I believe that the benefits proposed by this legislation are already available under section 72 of the Income Tax Act. It seems to me that here we are proposing to make grants available before the research has been done. Under the Income Tax Act allowances made for research are made only after the research has been completed. In this case we are putting the cart before the horse and making grants before we know that the research will be carried out successfully and what results will be forthcoming. For this reason I am not at all sure I agree with the bill in its present form.
Another question comes to mind. Will these grants be made available to government corporations? Will concerns such as Polymer or
February 23, 1967

Atomic Energy of Canada be eligible for giants under this measure? I should also like to know what is intended in cases which are the reverse of those I outlined a few moments ago. What will happen when a grant is made to a Canadian company which has a subsidiary in the United States? Would the subsidiary of the Canadian company qualify for a grant under this bill?
I think the motive behind this legislation is good. The idea is not new but it is being put forward in a new way. We are proceeding along lines different from those indicated in section 72 of the Income Tax Act. These questions may be answered as we study the bill clause by clause but the minister may wish to make a few general remarks before we leave clause 2 to assure the Canadian taxpayers and the committee that we are putting this money to proper use, that it will be well spent and spent for the purpose for which it is intended.
Personally, I would prefer that these grants be made only after the research and development work has been done. In my view this would be preferable to making a grant and saying: Here is your money, see what you can do with it. Suppose the money is spent without satisfactory results. The project fades away. Is there any provision for the return of whatever was provided by way of a grant?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO CORPORATIONS FOR RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think we all agree that the question of scientific research with which the bill before us purports to deal is one which concerns not only members of the House of Commons but the scientific community and industry as a whole throughout Canada. We are concerned because we know that Canada has been doing so little in this field compared with other modern industrialized countries.
Speaking on this subject about two weeks ago I compared government expeditures in the field of scientific research in Canada with government expenditures of other countries in this area. I pointed out that the United States government was spending approximately 3 per cent of its gross national product on research and development while Canada was spending less than 1 per cent. In his introductory remarks while moving the second reading of the bill the minister confirmed what I said with respect to government expenditures on research and told the house that the same disparity was to be found in expenditures by the private sector. On
Research
December 20 as reported at page 11433 of Hansard, the minister said:
Looking at the structure of our over-all scientific activity we find that industry performed only 36 per cent of the national total as contrasted with 63 per cent for Britain and 74 per cent in the United States. This anomaly in allocation of effort would indicate that insufficient emphasis is being placed on the practical exploitation of science and technology.
A little later he stated:
It would appear that a target almost three times the current figure is required to bring Canada more nearly into line with comparable industrialized countries. The attainment of this target within a reasonable period of time would require a virtual doubling of the previous long-term growth rate for industrial research and development.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
It seems to me, to judge from the speeches the minister has made on this subject, that he has formed an opinion as to the reasons for Canada's backwardness so far as expenditure on research is concerned. The reasons are not hard to find. So far as industry is concerned our present situation has arisen because such a large percentage of Canadian industry is owned by foreign investors, many of them in the United States, who tend, as they have tended in the past, to do their research at their head offices or in research centres outside this country. This is true not only of United States companies but of international concerns such as Shell Oil. It is also caused by the fact that companies and industries in Canada which are not foreign owned tend to be smaller and do not have the necessary financial resources to expand scientific and research development.
Since 1962 we have had a whole series of programs. We have had financial incentives and we have had tax rebates. We have had proposals for direct grants. It seems to me the reason we have had changes almost every year is simply that we have not given the basic and detailed consideration to the problem which is required. Also, we have not evolved a program which will meet our needs. I am not suggesting that such a program can be evolved in one week, one month or one year. What I am suggesting is that it is necessary to consult with the best brains and with those persons who are most highly trained in this field. We need to evolve a program so that in five or ten years' time we will attain the goal we want to attain. It seems to me that we will not achieve this aim if we have changes from year to year. I suggest that if we are to have changes from year to year we will inhibit the desire and the ability of Canadian industries to become involved in research.

February 23, 1967
Research
In making some notes along this line I came across an article which I presume the minister must have seen. It appeared in yesterday's Globe and Mail. The title of the article is "Is Ottawa Helping Or Hindering Development? A Wrench In the Research Machinery". The article goes into detail. I do not intend to read all of it into the record. It is based on an interview with Dr. J. J. Green, director of research for Litton System (Canada) Limited. I should like to read a couple of paragraphs which I think summarize fairly what Dr. Green thinks of this bill. He says:
The Canadian government appears to be taking away with one hand tax incentives to industry that it has been giving with the other.
Dr. Greene say that Bill C-252, now before the House of Commons, will reduce the tax advantage certain companies gained through research and development in previous years.
The article continues:
This means that the rewards are only for companies whose yearly expenditures are rising steeply, Dr. Green says. A company doing a fair level of research and development that did not increase in any one year would get nothing.
Dr. Green said in an interview, that schemes to encourage research in industry that have been initiated by the government during the past three or four years have had good response. Despite the encouraging results, the government proposes to change the basis on which these incentives rest.
The courrent interpretation of the proposed regulations is that they will be less favourable than the old regulations to industries that originally expanded their research and development capabilities-the very companies the government was first trying to encourage. Dr. Green says.
I could go on and on but I think the first two paragraphs indicate the fact that here is a research director of a company who feels that industrial research is being inhibited by the changes from year to year so that no company can make long-term plans. The minister and the country have had a great deal of advice about what we ought to do. I have here a report of a speech made by Dr. J. H. Chapman, deputy superintendent of the federal defence research telecommunications establishment, in which he said:
-the United States has been able to establish an industry of discovery because it has developed close links between the industrial and academic communities.
The articles goes on to say that the United States is calling for a national science policy. This was in May of 1965. The Ontario Research Foundation more than a year ago recommended the sitting up of a series of co-operative institutes to serve various fields

of industry under the over-all direction of a crown corporation. They point out the need for high level co-ordination to prevent wasteful duplication of effort among the associations. They propose that the cost of these institutes be split 50-50 between government and industry. They point out that Canada has limited funds to expend on industrial technology and every dollar must count.
The Ontario Research Foundation suggests that the associations themselves should recognize that Canada already has adequate facilities for basic research and should concentrate on meeting the need for ways of applying new knowledge more effectively. At the University of British Columbia they are discussing the setting up of research parks. The Financial Post of March 19 reports as follows:
Although primarily sponsored by the provincial government, the B.C. Research Council has been supported financially by many private corporations which have called upon it to carry out scientific and engineering projects which they were unable to do themselves.
The point I am endeavouring to make is that I believe this bill does not go far enough. The fact that the minister is bringing in another proposal this year, as he did last year and the year before, is an indication that the minister and the government still have not worked out a long-range policy. I suggest to the minister that the government must play a much more important role than it has in the past. It must not only encourage industries to do more research and development than they have in the past but also must work out methods, through financial incentives and tax rebates, to help them do this.
I should like to see the industries do research in co-operation with the National Research Council and other government agencies. Industry should also consult with the universities which finally, after many years, are now beginning to do a great deal more research and a great deal more training in the post-graduate field than they ever have done in the past. I believe the government should try to work out programs under which small businesses and industries can do research. They simply do not have the funds to do it on their own. They should be encouraged to work together in fields of research in which they have common purposes.
What I am trying to say is that there is a need to rationalize the research which is being done by industry and that the government should devise methods, which I do not see in this bill, to bring together individual companies in a particular industry so that they can
February 23, 1967

all benefit by doing research together. If they benefit, certainly the country as a whole will benefit. When I read this bill and compare it with the study done for the Economic Council in December, 1965, entitled "Program To Encourage Research And Development In Canadian Industry", it seems fairly obvious to me that the general principles worked out in that study have not been adopted by the government and certainly are not included in the provisions of the bill which the minister is proposing today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO CORPORATIONS FOR RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my contribution to this debate will be a very limited one, particularly since the hon. member for Winnipeg North has made most of the points I would have made. As he said, there is not sufficient research being done in Canada, particularly by companies which for the most part are controlled outside the country. I should like to commend the minister for bringing forward Bill No. C-252, because it differs in at least one fundamental aspect from the present legislation. I believe this point was touched on briefly by the hon. member for Wellington South. In the past young firms, particularly those not in a profitable position or not making any real profit after paying taxes, have not benefited from the tax incentive that has been available to other firms doing research. It is quite conceivable that during the years 1962 to 1966 certain companies engaged in research were unable to take advantage of the financial incentives of the government in view of the fact that they were operating at a loss.
I believe that Bill No. C-252, by substituting direct grants for tax rebates, makes it possible for the Minister of Industry to help finance industrial research in those companies which are still in their formative years and are not yet in a position to generate a net profit. I believe that in this particular instance the language in the bill is an improvement. I am sure the minister will wish to elaborate a little further on this subject.
There is, of course, another feature in this bill to which I believe the hon. member for Wellington South referred. I have only had an opportunity to read the bill once and I must admit that I did not attend the hearings of the committee. I understand, however, that the bill is designed to prod big business particularly to accelerate the research it is doing and invest more money in research.
There has been a tendency on the part of big companies to carry on year in and year out at the same fixed rate of investment in
Research
research, secure in the knowledge that a good portion of the cost of this research would be borne by the federal government. In the existing regulations there is very little if any incentive, other than the incentive, of course, to discover something of importance, to induce these companies to accelerate or increase their annual expenditure in the field of research. I imagine that this bill may go a long way toward encouraging companies to plan long-range research programs on an accelerated basis and with increased expenditures from year to year so that they make take full advantage of the provisions of this legislation.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Like the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, I have been a member of the food and drug committee for three and a half years. In that committee I have tried to be as objective as possible. It is a very difficult committee for a layman. But I have been made aware, by practically every brief presented to that committee by well established firms and relatively new and smaller firms, of the amount of research that these firms are undertaking and indeed must undertake if, according to their briefs, they are to continue to be vigorous and profitable. In other words, the drug industry claims I think with a certain amount of justification, that their industry perhaps more than any other depends upon the fruits of basic and applied research.
I think this industry can make a very excellent case for the amount of money it spends on an international level. But as I listened to their witnesses and experts and read their briefs I found they made only a very pathetic case for the amount of money they spend in this country on applied and basic research. If time permitted and if that committee was not in the midst of preparing its report to the house, I would discuss this in a little more depth. For instance, I would have pointed out to hon. members the experience in Australia where, because of incentives and inducements by the government of that country, the pharmaceutical industry has become a very vigorous exporter of products made there. By reason of the fact that we are situated so close to the United States I suppose the subsidiaries in this country of such companies have not found it profitable to carry out as much research or manufacturing here as I think they should have done. I can only hope that the Minister of Industry will take note of my remarks and see whether in the future some way cannot be found to make

February 23, 1967
Research
I hope through incentives and inducements but if necessary through punitive action, these international firms in the pharmaceutical industry, spend a little more of their research dollars right here in Canada.
When they present the balance sheets of their operations in this country they include a very healthy expenditure under the term "research and development." If the Canadian taxpayer is expected to pay for that research and development every time he swallows an aspirin or other pill, I think a little more of the research should be carried out in this country. Some of these industries, particularly in the pharmaceutical field, have been good, corporate Canadian citizens, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce likes to evaluate a company. They hire thousands of employees and spend millions of dollars in this country on wages and materials. But I think they are too prone to depend upon research facilities situated in such countries as Switzerland, the United States, England and Germany.
In this modern world where communications are so sophisticated I do not think there is any reason why research, particularly in the pharmaceutical industry, should not become more diversified and originate in Canada. There are exceptions, of course. I would not want to resume my seat and leave the impression that I have been making a blanket condemnation of the pharmaceutical industry in so far as research is concerned because there are firms such as Ayerst McKenna and Harrison Ltd. which are undertaking research in this country. This firm is carrying out research in the Montreal area for its parent company. I believe there are companies located in Sheridan Park, Toronto, which are increasing their research facilities. I understand that the pharmaceutical industry in Toronto and Montreal in particular is investing more money in research facilities and therefore helping to prevent the brain drain with which we are very familiar.
Nevertheless, Mr. Minister, I am one who is not satisfied with the amount of research carried out in this country by this industry. I have never believed in curing a nose-bleed by cutting off one's head, and I do not believe this is the approach that should be taken with respect to the pharmaceutical industry. I doubt that there is time to discuss the industry in general, but I think it should be made aware of the fact that while we recognize the necessity of international research and realize that in most instances the average Canadian is able to take advantage of the fruits of

international research, more research should be carried out in Canada.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
We realize also that in most instances the average Canadian is able to take advantage of the fruits of international research by the constant introduction of new medicines and new drugs. Nevertheless we deserve from these firms a greater share of their research dollar, particularly in view of the fact that a respectable amount of money goes out of this country to subsidize and help support international research facilities which exist in Pearl River, in the United States and at Basle, Switzerland.
There is a particular clause in this bill on which I will say a few words. It helps to achieve what I think is a desirable aim, namely, that the pharmaceutical industry, perhaps more than any other industry because it is so research-oriented, should do much more to spend in Canada some of the dollars which Canadian taxpayers pay for its products.
I want to commend the minister for the real increase in the field of research since 1962. I have never had an opportunity to speak in the House of Commons on legislation sponsored by the present Minister of Industry, perhaps because of the fact that for geographical reasons my interests are not centred on the auto pact but on other matters. However, I have been rather impressed by the performance of the minister who, perhaps more than any other minister of the government, has shown a willingness to try out new ideas and approaches. I could mention many of them but the chairman might rule me out of order. One of them is the auto pact which, although controversial, was an attempt to introduce a new approach to a vexing problem. Although it has resulted in much labour unrest and disruption it has also resulted in a significant sum of money, $200 million, accruing to this country. I am rather pleased that research should fall into the orbit of the Minister of Industry who, ever since I have been here, has shown no reluctance to try out new ways and means. This should be the new spirit in Canada because, after all, we are an extremely young nation.
I would have liked to spend a little time talking about the "brain drain", as we like to call it.
I should also like to commend to hon. members an article in today's Globe and Mail
February 23, 1967

entitled "New Grants For University Research" because I think the program is ancillary to the present bill. The article refers to a new basic approach by the National Research Council and it is a very encouraging ancillary measure in respect of the bill before us. In other words, it seems that through the National Research Council grants will be made available for university research.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North said, this has been an area in which action has been woefully lacking. The percentage of our gross national product devoted to basic and applied research in no way compares with that of countries like the United States and Australia, but I think that we are at least moving in the right direction. I read in the Financial Post that at present the rate of acceleration is such that by 1970-71 we will have reached the desirable goal set by the Economic Council and will be in line with other affluent nations.
In this connection I commend to the attention of hon. members a paper written by Roger Gaudry, rector of the University of Montreal, concerning the brain drain. I think it is an important paper because it erases some of the misconceptions under which many of us have laboured about the well known fact that so many of our well trained scientists and researchers leave Canada to go to the United States. According to Dr. Gaudry, based on information that he has acquired from Washington, from the Department of Labour here in Ottawa and from other available statistics, from 1956 to 1961 Canada lost to the United States an average of 212 scientists and 1,028 engineers per year, making a total average of 1,240 trained personnel. Expressed as a ratio of the 1959 output of science and engineering graduates, Canada lost on the average 12.5 per cent of its output of scientists and-this is staggering- 48 per cent of its output of engineers.
However, to my surprise, and perhaps to the surprise of Dr. Gaudry, because of immigration from Europe we have actually ended up with an over-all gain. According to recent figures that have been made available to me by the research division of the Department of Labour many Canadian trained personnel are now coming back to Canada. However, Dr. Gaudry made the very valid point that this is no reason to feel complacent. We should not be complacent about the fact that we are training university students who leave Canada to go to the United States, simply because we offset this loss by replacing them 23033-847
Research
with new Canadians. This type of compensation is bound to dry up as opportunities for work arise in the countries from which these people come and as their governments emphasize the necessity of keeping their professional people at home.
However, Dr. Gaudry made another valid point, namely, that the only way in which Canada can remain prosperous, in spite of the fact that it is situated next to an industrial giant, is to have something a little different to sell. We cannot succeed on the basis of price alone. We must have something uniquely Canadian to sell in the field of industry, and the best way to ensure that our products are wanted throughout the world and to make certain that our exports increase from year to year is to increase our support of industrial research so that we can come up with products that are really Canadian and not facsimiles of something developed in the United States or Great Britain.
I am sure that because of the abundance of our national resources there are particular areas to which our research should be directed. Our patent system will have a lot to do with it, and I would take a dim view of anyone who would want to destroy that system.
I agree with previous speakers that perhaps this bill is not the end to all our problems in the field of research, but I think it is a very helpful step forward because it forces the large companies not only to maintain their present research facilities but to spend more money from year to year thus accelerating their efforts. Second, through the medium of this bill some financial compensation will now be made available to those firms which, for taxation reasons, in previous years were unable to take advantage of the tax incentives.
I once again ask the Minister of Industry to take note of my remarks, and I also hope that the pharmaceutical industry will do so. While I commend it for what it has already done in the field of research I hope it will continue and increase its efforts. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this subject was discussed at some length in the committee. I am sorry the hon. member for Wellington South did not have the opportunity of being there. The object of this bill is to encourage industrial research in Canada in the expectation and hope it will improve Canadian industrial technology and consequently raise the standard of living. We specify in the bill that in order to qualify for a grant the applicant must have carried out research in Canada. The grants are payable only in retrospect, that is, after the research has been carried out and some auditing has been done of the quantum of research. In addition, before the grant is paid there will be insistence vis-a-vis the grantee that the grantee is free to exploit the outcome of the research, if it is successful, in Canada.
[Mr. Mackasey.l
I do not believe one can have a bill such as this, designed to encourage research, and state in advance in relation to a program that may take five years to bring to fruition that whatever the result of this research may be it will be exploited exclusively in Canada or that if a product is the outcome it will be manufactured in Canada. It may be uneconomic to manufacture in Canada by reason of the scale of production, technological difficulties, lack of proper machinery and so on. This would mean that one would be discouraging or closing off the advancement of a number of avenues for research in Canada which may otherwise be attractive. Consequently you would be doing what the hon. member for Winnipeg North mentioned, taking away with one hand what you are giving with another.

Indeed, if he is free to do so and it is economic to exploit the research in Canada, it is obviously in his interests to exploit it in Canada. We expect this to follow as a consequence. subtopic: GEOGRAPHICAL CO-ORDINATES RESPECTING BASE LINES

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, February 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Barnett:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this house a copy of all notes and other communications exchanged between Canada and the United States of America since the enactment by parliament on July 16, 1964, of the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act having to do with the issuance by the Governor in Council of one or more lists of geographical co-ordinates of points from which base lines may be determined in accordance with the provisions of the act.

subtopic: GEOGRAPHICAL CO-ORDINATES RESPECTING BASE LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this motion is one that has held the attention of members from coastal constituencies and others for some years now, and in fact interest in our territorial sea predates by many years the enactment of the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act. The motion before us seeks to have certain papers tabled and made public, namely, documents, letters, etc., exchange between the Canadian government and the government of the United States with regard to Canada taking action through the governor in council under law of this parliament to establish geographical co-ordinates from which straight base lines would be drawn and from which would be measured our territorial sea and o ur fishing zones.
I realize that on a motion such as this we are normally confined to discussing the possibility and necessity or otherwise of tabling the documents and it is not a motion dealing with the substance of the matter at all. But in this instance I think to reason for the production of the documents one must touch upon the subject matter and relate some historical events in so far as the subject matter is concerned. This was recognized by

the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and Mr. Speaker on the last day this motion was debated. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said in part, as reported on page 12860 of Hansard for February 9 last:
However, I understand the interest of the two hon. gentlemen and other members of this house in the substance of the proposition, and therefore 1 have not raised a point of order.
This means that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, knowledgeable as he is about the intimate workings of parliament, realized the necessity of discussing the substance of this matter. When I say that Mr. Speaker at least, condoned that approach I mean he did so by not intervening and by recognizing the overriding importance of being able to look at the substance of the question in order to reason whether the documents should be produced. This is what I hope to do this evening.
My colleague the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), as a member from British Columbia and one who is very interested in this and many other fishing matters, gave a very laudable and commendable outline of the subject in his opening remarks. The hon. member pointed out very clearly the degree to which the government has been negligent in this matter in not carrying out the responsibilities which parliament gave it. I should like to quote further the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs because I think they reveal an attitude which should not have as much scope and force in the determinations of government as it has. As reported at page 12860 of Hansard the minister said:
I do understand, however, the impatience of hon. gentlemen.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs was referring to impatience over the delay in the governor in council proclaiming the geographical co-ordinates. He said:
I share that impatience, and so does the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) who has toiled arduously during the past two and a half years in an effort to implement the full provisions of the bill.
I do not have the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act before me but in it the responsibility is given to the governor in council to proclaim either in whole or in part the geographical co-ordinates for Canada. We wonder why there has been such arduous toil for two and a half years in order to implement these geographical co-ordinates. What are the difficulties? I can understand that
February 23, 1967

there might be some difficulties when a number of other countries have historic fishing rights and make claim to the right to fish within the 12-mile limit, whether it be one that follows the convolutions of the coast or a straight line. I can understand the difficulties when there are a number of nations making this claim, because this is the case on the Atlantic coast. I can understand those difficulties when there is a desire by the government of Canada to have those nations phase out their historic fishing rights so that after a certain period of time they will no longer have the right to fish within the 12-mile zone.
In respect of the Atlantic coast there may be an argument for such protraction because there are a number of countries concerned in this question, some of whom have treaty fishing rights. That matter was dealt with at length by my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni before the committee and in this house on a previous occasion. Portugal, France, Spain, Denmark and other countries, I believe, claim these historic fishing rights.
My concern here is with the substance of this matter in so far as the Pacific coast is concerned. On the Pacific coast only one country claims to have historic fishing rights within the 12-mile limit and the area about which the Fisheries Association, the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union and everybody in the fishing industry in British Columbia has a unanimous opinion. Queen Charlotte Sound, Hecate Strait and Dixon Entrance fall within the area they claim should be inside the straight base lines. Only one country, the United States, claims historic fishing rights within this area.
The United States' claims have been recognized because the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), at the meeting in Hyannis Port with the late President Kennedy to which the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred in his remarks of February 9, guaranteed to President Kennedy that he need have no fear about the historic fishing rights of the United States within the area which would be encompassed by our 12-mile fishing zone. The Prime Minister said we would recognize those rights. This information was given to the Senate, to the house and to the committee on marine and fisheries which was then considering the territorial sea and fishing zones bill. This information was given to us on a number of occasions by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud). These ministers said that Canada would recognize that historic fishery,
Motions for Papers
namely, the bottom fishery of United States fishermen in the area which would be within the 12-mile fishing zone as contemplated.
This being the case, and there being no indication that the government intended to ask the United States to phase out its fishing operation in that area off the Pacific coast-in other words, we would recognize in perpetuity their historic right-what is the subject of negotiations with the United States in this respect? The only thing which can be the subject of negotiations is the location of the geographical co-ordinates. The responsibility for setting those geographical co-ordinates has been given to the governor in council, but we are presumably negotiating the location of the straight base lines and the geographical co-ordinates with the United States of America. I submit it is none of the blessed business of the United States of America where those straight base fines and geographical co-ordinates are drawn. It is a determination that Canada, as a sovereign state unto itself, should make.
When the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act was progressing through the house there were great declarations that Canada would be firm and resolute and would make a unilateral declaration and decision on this matter. It was said that it was commendable for a country such as Canada to be able to make this sort of declaration in the face of world conditions at that time, a time before the United States decided to take action with respect to the 12-mile limit and a time of conflict between Iceland and Great Britain on the subject of fishing zones and the territorial sea.
In the fight of those firm determinations and expressions by the government, we cannot help but wonder what is the purpose of the negotiations. I think that without even seeing the correspondence we must come to the conclusion that the United States government wants these geographic co-ordinates and straight base fines to be as close as possible to the mainland of the west coast of Canada, as opposed to the position which the government took before the marine and fisheries committee, namely, that the geographical co-ordinates would be as far seaward as possible. In other words, it was said that the geographical co-ordinates would follow the brief presented to the committee by the Fisheries Association.
The brief of that association had in it a map or chart of the west coast and the Atlantic coast. The chart of the west coast indicated that the geographical co-ordinates and the straight base fines would proceed from a

February 23, 1967
Motions for Papers
point on the international boundary in Juan de Fuca Strait, off the west coast of Vancouver Island, in a direct line from the northwestern tip of Vancouver Island near Cape Scott, or the outermost island off Cape Scott, thence to the southwestern tip of the Queen Charlotte Islands close to Cape St. James, thence along the west coast of the Queen Charlotte Islands to Langara or North Island and up to the international boundary which runs between British Columbia and Alaska. The Canadian government endorsed the position taken in the brief of the Fisheries Association. These geographical coordinates represented the hope of everyone involved in the fishing industry in British Columbia. It was the expectation of members of the committee that these geographical coordinates would be implemented.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
We were told that there- was no intention of asking the United States to phase out the historic fishery in that area. It was only intended to make the United States subject to our various fishery regulations, and what could be more reasonable than that? If we are only negotiating with the United States the application of Canadian fishery regulations to foreign fishing vessels operating inside our territorial sea and fishing zones, then I submit this should not be the subject of negotiations. If that is so, then what is being negotiated? Obviously what is being discussed is how far toward our coast the United States authorities can drive our own base lines. I submit that what the United States wants to do, for military or pseudo-military reasons or just to satisfy its massive ego, is to have as much of Queen Charlotte Sound, Hecate Strait and Dixon Entrance as possible, an area Which I thought was Canadian territory dating as far back as 1903 when a British tribunal made the decision regarding the boundary between British Columbia and Alaska.
I suggest that what the United States wants to do is to have as much as possible of what we now consider to be Canadian waters, even though we have no base lines drawn to enclose them, declared as international waters and outside of our fishery zone. I hope that the government is not negotiating away the concept and understanding which we have had on the west coast for many years about what are considered to be Canadian waters. It seems to me that the only prospect in sight is an adulteration or dilution of the position which the government took so firmly before

the fisheries committee when the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act was being considered. We attempted in that committee to spell out the geographic co-ordinates on the west coast and to have the base lines follow the position agreed to by everyone in the fishing industry in British Columbia, namely, to include those waters I have just mentioned, Hecate Strait, Dixon Entrance and Queen Charlotte Sound. However, we relented in the committee on the basis of the understanding given by responsible ministers of the crown that there would be no delay in proclaiming the geographic co-ordinates.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs said unequivocally, without hesitation and in clear language

I must say that is a remarkable distinction for him-that the geographic co-ordinates would be declared before the end of 1964. With that understanding members of the committee accepted the government's word and relented. Subsequently we have found that for the last two and a half or three years there has been a continuous exchange of proposals. Two or three times the Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Minister of Fisheries, whichever one happened to deal with the subject at the time, said that they were awaiting the reaction of the United States government to proposals made by the Canadian government. It is preposterous that such a situation should arise, that when the parliament of Canada has given to the governor in council authority to declare geographic co-ordinates and the governor in council has agreed to make proposals about where those co-ordinates should be the government should be making proposals to a foreign country about what we should do within our own territory. In other words, we are permitting the United States of America to decide where those geographic co-ordinates are going to be and what will be the fishing zones and the territorial sea of Canada on the west coast. However, so as not to trespass upon the good grace of the house I will end with a quotation dealing with the relationship between Canada and the United States. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said the following, as recorded on page 12861 of Hansard:
I believe that we should hear from the United States within the course of the next few days. When this reply reaches us we will have a better appreciation of when we can begin to establish co-ordinates and straight base lines, and when we may take other steps to further the objective we have in mind.
In other words, the minister said that everything rests upon the United States. This has been the answer we have received every time questions have been put to cabinet ministers. Time after time we have been told that all we have to do is to wait for the United States to reply to us, wait for them to tell us what they want, wait for them to agree or disagree with something we have proposed, and then we will know what to do. This is what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said just two weeks ago. It is a regrettable state of affairs when we allow a foreign country, which we have already agreed will have a perpetual right to fish within our fishing zones, to proceed to decide where our geographic co-ordinates will be. I would have thought this would be something that our government would be proud to do in its own sovereign way and declare for the benefit of all Canadians without having to report to the United States government and ask that government to decide what the Canadian government will do.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had an opportunity to listen to the remarks of the hon. members for Co-mox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) and Skeena (Mr. Howard). The hon. member for Skeena pointed out to us that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) recognized the particular interest of certain hon. members in discussing the subject matter of the 12-mile limit. However, at the same time the Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out quite clearly to the house that the issue before us at this time is not whether the government has made progress in these negotiations but whether the house should be given the documents which have been exchanged between the government of Canada 23033-848
Motions for Papers
and other governments. While I well recognize the concern and the impatience of the hon. member in this matter, I think it must be clearly understood that the course of action which is advocated in this motion is one that would be most irresponsible and in fact would not be in keeping with the custom so far as such documents are concerned.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
On the first day this matter was discussed, February 9, the minister cited a number of cases which pointed out the absolute necessity of the government not making public the documents in question. To do so, without consulting the other countries involved, would be an irresponsible act and, in fact, would serve no useful purpose. Before dealing with the motion before the house at this time, namely whether or not these documents should be produced, I want to reiterate that ample evidence has already been introduced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), and supported in a very reasonable speech by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean), that this would be an unjustifiable course of action.
I should like to refer to a remark made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) as recorded on page 12856 of Hansard:
While there may be times when I would readily agree that the kind of documents asked for in this motion could be properly considered as privileged and it might not be in the public interest to table them in the house, nevertheless I feel that under the particular set of circumstances prevailing in this case the general rule has in effect ceased to apply.
The hon. member and his colleagues have failed this afternoon to produce one iota of evidence to support in a technical or legal way the reasoning behind that statement. They have pointed out that there was impatience as a result of the fact that the ultimate question has not been resolved. I would not want to say this until I have had an opportunity of rereading the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), but I think he might have been a little unfair to the minister when he said he was impatient. In my opinion, impatience is a state of mind, which I think is legitimate and understandable, when one is confronted with a difficult or complex situation. Then, I think one is apt to experience impatience. However, if one has that experience that does not mean the impatience is the result of procrastination or undue delay.

February 23, 1967
Motions for Papers
I should like to point out to the house that, notwithstanding the vital interest of the two members in question as well as my own interest and concern in this matter, I think they are being somewhat unrealistic. The hon. member for Skeena has said, if I recall correctly, that it was difficult for him to understand the situation. I find it difficult myself, having regard for the intellect and knowledge of the hon. member for Skeena, to comprehend the difficulties which he is having. I feel it should be apparent to him, perhaps more so than to many other members because of his experience in the house and his knowledge of this field, that when a country is engaged in international negotiations, by their very nature those negotiations are more intricate and more sensitive than any other negotiations that may take place within the country itself.
I think many of us have experienced impatience with things on the domestic scene; yet we know that government, in dealing with domestic problems, has a variety of matters to take into consideration such as legal claims or alleged legal claims or the interests of various groups. There is often a period of time between the date when the government decides on a particular course of action and the date when the desirable end is achieved. If these difficulties are experienced in the domestic field, then I think that is ample prima facie evidence that generally when one is engaged in international negotiations there is more involved. It may well be that in most cases such negotiations are more difficult and the desirable end is more difficult to achieve.
I should like to point out further to both hon. members that since 1964 when the legislation to which they have referred was introduced, we have, as a country, made progress in dealing with this matter. The hon. gentleman has talked at great length about the area that he represents. He made no mention in his speech of the effect that the legislation has had to date on foreign fleets. I am referring specifically to the operations of the Russians on the Atlantic coast, with which I am more familiar than I am with the Pacific coast.
Progress has been made, too, with regard to the Norwegian sealing operation in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. In the two and a half years which have passed since the introduction of this legislation, there have been other developments which, while they might not appear at this time to be of great consequence, are of such an order as to suggest to me that they are of significance. I refer to the action which

the United States has taken with regard to this problem, something which they did not seem either anxious or willing to do a few years ago.
There is one other matter I should like to mention while dealing with the over-all problem. I believe the hon. member for Skeena is off the point when he suggests that this is a matter of a foreign country dictating to another country the extent to which that country may exercise its jurisdiction. I remind the hon. member again that in the field of international relations Canada has certain responsibilities with regard to the International Court. I should like to think that the successful solution of this problem will be one that will stand the test of international law.
Again I say that all of us, particularly those of us who represent coastal regions, are very anxious that at the earliest possible date as much progress as is possible should be made. At the same time, while expressing this understandable impatience, we ought to keep what is involved in a proper perspective. I do feel the hon. member for Skeena is somewhat over-simplifying the problem. Again I say that while the hon. member who introduced this motion may have wished to express his views on the merits of the question, nevertheless he could not have been acting in a completely responsible manner because if the motion were to carry I suggest we would tend to jeopardize rather than assist the negotia-toins in which our constituents have such a great interest.
In view of the precedents cited by the minister, I believe all hon. members will recognize that it would be an unwise and irresponsible course of action to adopt this motion. I feel we have no course but to defeat it, and in so defeating it I think we will be rendering more assistance to the cause of achieving a desirable solution to this problem than if we were to carry the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I am always impressed by the eloquence of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) who can speak on labour, northern affairs, Indian affairs and the problems of fishing rights with equal facility. I do not say that sarcastically. I commend the hon. member. I can only commend to new members of the house that they take advantage of the private members hour to the same extent that the hon. member for Skeena through the years has taken
February 23, 1967

advantage of it, that they speak as he speaks, and develop that eloquence which I envy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: GEOGRAPHICAL CO-ORDINATES RESPECTING BASE LINES
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you were mesmerized by the hon. members' eloquence. Your Honour permitted the debate to centre around the 12-mile limit and the treaty-why the treaty has not been finalized and why co-ordinates have not been established-rather than on the issue of whether certain documents exchanged between the United States and Canada should be made available to members of the house. I suspect Your Honour was indulgent because there has not been enough opportunity to discuss this important piece of legislation in the last year or so.
Coming from the city of Verdun, I confess that my interest is not as devoted or developed as is the interest of the hon. member for Skeena. If I were to take a point 12 miles from my home area I might wind up somewhere in the next county.
Periodically the problem arises in this house as to the desirability of producing certain papers. There is a lack of clear definition of what is a privileged document and what is not. The process of having members of the house decide whether a document is or is not privileged by majority is not democratic, it seems to me. A forward step we ought to take would be to devise definite rules to guide members of the House of Commons as to what documents are or are not privileged. To decide whether documents should be made public by the process of one party out voting the other parties, is undemocratic, I suspect. If we look at it closely, I suspect we shall see that this further restricts the freedom of the average member in the house. I know the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) shares my viewpoint.
As I have said before, we can only go by precedent in deciding whether a document is privileged. There are no guide lines. This matter ought to concern the special committee that will look into procedural reform. Other countries have specific norms to follow, and it is time we had some rule of thumb to decide these matters other than a straight majority of the house, or a vote.
In England there is a tendency to consider all documents privileged. With few exceptions, in England they consider all documents privileged. Hon. members interested in doing a little research in the library will find that in 23033-8481
Motions for Papers
England privileged documents cover almost all documents issued by the government. They include for instance transactions between the government and private contractors. As an observer of the English scene it seems to me that the concept of privilege over there restricts the basic rights of the average member of parliament. The rights of the average citizen are indirectly infringed upon. At the other extreme we have the situation in Sweden.
The time has come, I think, for a special committee of the house objectively to look at the question of documents. That committee could investigate the English and Swedish systems, to see which one is better suited to our parliamentary system.
In passing may I say that our committees have given backbenchers an opportunity to take an active part in affairs. The committees system has removed much of the frustration which might otherwise ensue. One effect of the committees, it seems to me, has been to curtail the importance and prestige of the House of Commons. In the final analysis the House of Commons protects us against an undemocratic system of government. We must find ways and means of best using the committee system and at the same time restoring and maintaining the image of the House of Commons. A committee ought to settle this question about documents, and make some recommendations. Those problems ought to be decided objectively, and the minority parties not constantly penalized for their lack of members. However, I do not say that that is the situation here.
I expect most hon. members know about the Swedish system in which, contrary to the English system, with a few exceptions, all documents are considered public. In the main cities of Sweden the government has set up reading rooms in city halls and libraries, where many documents considered privileged in Canada, and certainly in England, are available to the public. It is not uncommon to see in the evening, or on a Saturday morning, political science students, newspapermen, interested senior citizens and others poring over those documents in reading rooms scattered throughout Sweden. Every person can be familiar with the every day workings of his government or parliament. This does much to alleviate the burden on an ombudsman in a country where this enlightened official operates.
The solution to our difficulties in Canada must lie, I think, in a happy medium. In a

February 23, 1967
Motions for Papers
country such as ours, where the press in unbridled, there are occasions when, if documents were made available weekly or daily, too much might be read into them, particularly by people who are subjective and not objective.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
I know this would not be the case in this instance. I am sure that is these documents were made available to the hon. member for Skeena and his partner they would be put to very objective use-the hon. members are really interested in finding out why it should take so much time to finalize a piece of legislation which is highly desirable to the fishing industry of this country.
I must not be tempted to enter upon a discussion as to the desirability of a 12-mile limit and the desirability of a speedy settlement with the United States. I must stick to the issue before us, which is whether or not these documents exchanged between the Canadian government and the United States are to be considered as privileged. I will admit I have no means of knowing whether or not they are privileged. I must take the word of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) for that. Luckily, my hon. friend has such a wonderful reputation in all parts of the house that I am sure all hon. members will accept such an assurance from him without question.
My impression is that the hon. members who raised this matter were interested not so much in the production of these papers as they were in the opportunity to discuss this whole subject at length, in an effort to ascertain why a solution to this vexing problem has not so far been reached.

words-an exception should be made in this case.
Obviously the hon. member admits that in normal circumstances these papers are privileged. As I listened to the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) I failed to find anything in his eloquent remarks which persuaded me that there was anything extraordinary about this particular situation which would make the tabling of these papers desirable.
The question before us is not whether the co-ordinates should have been determined three months, six months or a year ago. This is a complex matter, as the former minister of fisheries rightly pointed out during his participation in the debate not long ago. The real question is whether or not these papers are privileged. I can only repeat that in the opinion of the Secretary of State for External Affairs they are privileged documents. They embody correspondence between the governments of two countries and I am afraid that even in the most ideal of circumstances the Secretary of State for External Affairs would have to obtain permission from the United States before there could be any question of tabling them.
I believe both members of the New Democratic Party have done service to the house by emphasizing once again the lack of guidance from which the house suffers when approaching such problems. to what should be considered privileged and what should not.

Mr. Chairman, I commend the efforts of the hon. member for Winnipeg North in trying to get more research done by research associations, in universities and in similar institutions. However, perhaps there are some objections to the technique that he has proposed to bring this about. I might say in the first place that federal government support for research in universities and other non-profit organizations is provided through a number of channels other than this bill. Perhaps the best known one is the National Research Council, and in this connection I will refer the hon. gentleman to the current issue of the Globe and Mail which, at page 25, attempts to summarize the past performance and anticipates the vastly increased performance of the N.R.C. in this matter of support for universities, and a new technique which they are proposing to adopt to achieve this. [DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Second, the Department of Industry has recently inaugurated a new program which is called, support of industrial research institutes. We are now starting in two universities, as an initial step, to organize non-profit research institutes which will encourage and engage in self-sustaining research with industry, with a view both to bringing the industrial community closer to the university in the research field and of providing a focus for having research done with facilities which, as the hon. gentleman pointed out, small businesses cannot afford.
It would be the hope that by meeting some elements of the administrative costs of these new institutes there could be a considerable increase in industrial research done by universities in universities, with facilities of a calibre which small businesses themselves could not afford. I think probably this is a better approach than the one suggested in this amendment.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I do think that there would be a danger, were this amendment adopted, that large corporations now engaged in research on their own account with their own facilities, would quite obviously quickly organize this same research under an institute of some description and thereby double the federal grant without changing the quantum or nature of the research at all. I do not believe one would want to encourage this kind of manoeuvre.

February 23, 1967
Research

My question in part arises from a question I asked before the dinner recess. Advice whether research into the fields of air, water and soil pollution are likely to be of benefit to Canada is not, I suggest, obtainable particularly from the Department of Trade and Commerce. speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED

I think the observation just made is a very useful one. The drafting of 12 (b) indicates clearly the significance which would be given to the phrase "of benefit to Canada". The test which was to be applied and which had to be satisfied was that the corporations engaging in research would be free from any kind of external inhibition against exploiting the research in Canada, whether this be an economic law of another jurisdiction outside Canada, whether it be an agreement between the company doing research in Canada and some foreign company outside Canada, or whether it be a matter of corporate policy in a parent-subsidiary relationship. It was felt that the best source of this information would be the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) do not limit the minister in his search for advice to those particular departments. The object of the provision is rather to place an obligation upon
[Mr. Bamett.l
those departments to provide advice. They do not limit the minister to those particular sources for the information he may require. If a question should arise as to whether pollution research of a particular nature is likely to be beneficial, there is nothing here to inhibit the seeking of advice from the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources or, indeed, from any other department.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of National Revenue and President of the Treasury Board) moved
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF VARIOUS ACTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF OFFICIALS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-266, to provide for the revision of certain salaries fixed by statute.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill before us is, I think, largely self-explanatory. Its principal purpose is to bring up to date the salaries of certain officers whose remuneration is fixed by statute and cannot be changed except by legislative action. The last occasion on which the salaries in question were changed was in December, 1963, when a special enactment, chapter 41 of the Statutes of Canada 1963, was approved by parliament, covering much the same group of officials as those with whom this present bill is concerned.
The bill now before the house incorporates also one new principle, applicable to some but not all the officers whose salaries will be adjusted by this statute. It seeks the authority of parliament to enable the governor in council to make future salary adjustments of most of the officers covered by this legislation without the requirement of returning to parliament to seek further legislative amendments. Exceptions are made in the case of three officials who bear a special relationship to parliament, the Auditor General, the Chief Electoral Officer and the Representation Commissioner. In these three cases the special relationship which exists between these three officers and parliament suggests that changes in their rate of remuneration should continue to be made only with the express legislative authority of parliament.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
In all other cases, however, except that of the Commissioner General for Canadian government participation in Expo '67-which post will disappear at the end of the World Fair or shortly after-there would appear to be justification for asking for a release from the requirement that the executive must come back to parliament and seek legislative amendments, either through an omnibus bill or through a whole series of separate amendments, every time a salary increase appears to be justified.
I trust that hon. members on all sides of the house will agree with the government's proposals for expediting the salary treatment of the officials covered by the bill. The fact

that their rates of remuneration have remained frozen since December 1, 1963 and that they can be changed only as a result of legislative action by parliament, now long overdue, indicates the nature of the problem. With the legislative work-load that has faced parliament in recent years, and is likely to continue into the future, there would appear to be little justification for adding to parliament's agenda unnecessarily through bills such as these whose sole purpose is to authorize a periodic increase in the salaries of certain officers of boards, commissions, etc.
Further, it is not fair to the officers concerned, in the view of the government, to ask them to accept the long delays in salary adjustments that arise from the existing legislative requirement, especially in times like the present ones when outside salaries are moving upward with abnormal rapidity, and all other public servants, including all deputy ministers and many other members of commissions, boards, etc. can have their salaries kept current and reasonably up to date by executive action.
Members will wish to know the basis on which the proposed increases have been recommended. When deputy ministers', and other order in council salaries were adjusted last to bring them up to date from December 1, 1963 to December 1, 1965, an increase of 8 per cent was determined as the basis for most of those adjustments. The same percentage has been adopted in most of the cases covered by the legislation. Exceptions to the general rule have been made in a number of cases, notably the Auditor General, the vice chairman of the National Energy Board, and the first vice chairman of the Tariff Board, in recognition of the fact that their existing rates of pay do not reflect adequately the measure of their duties and/or the special responsibilities which they are carrying.
In the case of the Auditor General, the amount of increase has also been set in recognition of the fact that any future salary adjustments in his case will require parliamentary action and can only be considered when the Financial Administration Act is undergoing amendment. The effective date for all increases goes back to December 1965-that is the date of the increase for senior civil servants. I should also add that there are certain restraints placed by the bill on the freedom of the governor in council to make further salary adjustments in future. No authority is given for reductions in salary by action of the governor in council. Safeguards
February 23, 1967
are provided to ensure internal relativity and equality of treatment among all ordinary members within each board and commission.
I will be glad to elaborate on these and other points which may be of interest to hon. members when we reach the clause by clause discussion of the bill. Meanwhile, I hope that the explanations I have given will suffice to satisfy the house that it can give approval in principle to the bill at this stage.

Mr. Speaker, the bill now before the house involves a major change in principle. Heretofore a substantial number of salaries were fixed only by statute and the governor in council had no authority in respect of them. As I understand it, the principle behind that practice was simply to assure the total independence of the members of these boards from the governor in council or from any direct or indirect pressure by the cabinet. In this bill we are making a change and putting it within the authority of the cabinet to increase salaries, although the legislation provides a floor. If the house is aware of this major change in principle and is satisfied that there is not likely to arise as a result thereof any type of direct or indirect pressure upon these public servants, then there could be no complaint. I might have understood it more readily if this had applied right across the board in all statutory salaries, but the minister has indicated that there are exemptions in relation to three cases which he says bear a very special relationship to parliament, namely the Auditor General, the Representation Commissioner and the Chief Electoral Officer. I have some reservations as to whether their intimacy with the work of parliament is of such a nature that it justifies a differentiation from the other categories set forth in the schedule to the bill.
Perhaps the proper time to discuss this with the minister will be in committee of the whole, but I think the minister will have to put before the committee some more cogent reasons than he has already given as to why we should abandon what has been the time honoured procedure of fixing salaries by statute and thereby protecting totally the impartiality and independence of these particular boards and commissions.
I know there are problems which arise by reason of the delay in getting around to the matter, but even those delays can be taken care of when the legislation is made substantially retroactive, as is the case here.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PORTUGAL-REPORTED INTENTION TO EXILE POLITICAL PRISONERS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PORTUGAL-REPORTED INTENTION TO EXILE POLITICAL PRISONERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 14 I inquired of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) whether the government intended to make any representations to the government of Portugal about the recent introduction of a decree providing for the exile from metropolitan Portugal of political prisoners. I am glad to have the opportunity to enlarge on the importance of this question. My question arose out of a recent trip taken by the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacDonald) and myself to Lisbon when we had the opportunity of interviewing a good many outstanding Portugese lawyers, writers, students and relatives of political prisoners.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
It is of course no news that Portugal has for many years-I think about 40 now-been governed by a dictatorship. Nor is it news that Portugal is a police state. What is not perhaps equally well known is that repression is growing worse and not, as in Spain, moderating. This may be, of course, because of increasingly adverse economic conditions which result, in part perhaps, from Portugal's involvement in three colonial wars in Africa.
On September 24 of last year, Mr. Speaker, a new decree was passed by the government of Portugal. It is No. 47216 and the substance of it is that the ministers of justice and overseas can authorize sentences or security measures issued by metropolitan courts-metropolitan courts are the courts in Portugal-or courts of the adjacent islands to be served in prison establishments overseas.
Now, Mr. Speaker, deportation or exile has long been a sinister weapon of dictatorship. This particular decree revives in Portugal, and amongst the many political prisoners and their families, the memories of a notorious concentration camp, the Tarrafal, in the Cape Verde Islands. Many people lost their lives or rotted away in these remote islands, forgotten, and where they could not very well be observed. The effect of this sort of decree is to separate people from their families and from any contact with the civilized world.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion That the government of Portugal is ashamed of this sort of decree is obvious from the fact that, although the decree is published in an official gazette, we were shown a newspaper which merely reprinted the decree without any comment, and this was crossed out by the censors so the people generally should not have it published to them.
It may be asked why we in Canada should be concerned. The reason is that we are an ally of Portugal in NATO. Both Canada and Portugal are bound by the treaty to safeguard the freedom, common heritage and civilization of their peoples founded on the principle of democracy, individual liberty and the rule of law. The callous disregard for the rule of law and the reversion to barbarism by coercing political prisoners reflects discredit not only on the particular country but on the whole western alliance which is supposed to be united in preserving certain basic human values. It may be said that the Portuguese authorities will know that Canada looks askance on methods of terrorism, that it would be unnecessary or useless for us to intervene or protest. It may be said the protests would be disregarded. We were assured many times that about the only thing that could influence the government of that country was international concern that was expressed.
Canada, I suggest, should base its protest on the terms of the NATO treaty and upon the universal declaration of human rights. We cannot in Canada shut our eyes to oppression, no matter where it happens to be. We should do something to prevent this infamous decree from being employed. We ought to make a protest that may well influence the government of that country which still desires to be considered civilized.
