speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, further to the question I put this morning with regard to some T.V. producers, I must say it is high time the minister stepped in.
You may object that the minister has nothing to say about the production of programs. I shall retort that it is up to him to protect the public, that it is his duty, a duty he cannot shirk.
I must admit we are pretty well fed up with some of the goings-on over T.V., and generally speaking, the Canadian people feel even more strongly about it than we do.
We have reached the point where we ask: Who is boss in this country of ours? Who makes the laws? Whose duty is it to see that those laws are respected? I ask you those same questions. Are you going to remain silent much longer before such disquieting radio and T.V. performances as we witness? Some T.V. producers seem to be using the network to spread subversive ideas.
During the past few years, this has too often been the case on our screens. Sometimes you have some immigrant from Cuba or other socialist country appearing, trying to make the population believe that the country he has left-probably because he could no longer stand it there-has the best system of government in the world. And the population believes these lies. In the first place, you will note that most of the revolutionary leaders are foreigners.
Later, our Canadian citizens appear on the screen, being granted free time by the authorities, taking pride in the fact that they are militant communists or revolutionary socialists.
They take the authority of running down all authorities with shouts of "Liberty"; they deny any authority; they engage in the most shameful immorality. And that is shown on
February 23, 1967	COMMONS
our screens, in our living rooms. Divorce is a daily pastime. The actors are often homosexuals performing on the stage with naked women in the background. And the feast goes on in an orgy beyond description in which our great alcoholics play their parts. Now, if some honest people-for there happen to be some honest people left in Canada-make the mistake of informing the authorities, our modern scatter-brains call them old-fashioned.
Today, through guilty indifference, if not implicit approval, which I would not dare believe, we are obviously heading toward a revolution. We are in a tower of Babel. Those who should use broadcasting facilities to inform the people have abdicated in favor of revolutionaries.
We say that consciously or not the present government is encouraging that situation -for instance by allowing a man called Bour-geault to talk on eight occasions on television and radio. And what did he have to say? That he is an agnostic, that is to say that he no longer believes in God or the devil and that he wants to lead a country made up of 80 per cent of Roman Catholics and Christians. And some applaud such aberration; it is enough to make one weep, Mr. Speaker.
On another occasion a student or a university professor will tell us that he is an atheist, a communist or a socialist and that only through revolution will Quebec gain her freedom.
Finally, another one comes with his children. He says proudly that he did not have them baptized to leave them free to choose their religion. Can you imagine a two-year old or a five-year old choosing his religion while waiting probably for the day when he will at last be able to choose his father or mother who never got married anyway? What a lovely generation.
Do you really believe it is with such individuals we are going to build a sound and strong society? I am therefore asking the hon. minister, on behalf of the Canadian people, to create as soon as possible a board of inquiry to do the housecleaning work that is needed in the C.B.C. Thank God, there are still several honest workers in the C.B.C., whose most ardent desire is to purge our sound-waves from the filth of society. The general welfare commands the attention of the hon. minister in that field and a delay would but aggravate such a discouraging situation. I am therefore urging him to act and to act quickly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Canada, thank God, we still live in a free country, and I hope we will never see the destiny of our country in the hands of a totalitarian and communist regime, as has and still is the unfortunate lot of several countries in the world.
In a free country, Mr. Speaker, all citizens should have freedom of thought and of speech and, like all taxpayers, they should be allowed to use the information media available.
In a free country, Mr. Speaker, the state cannot decently and logically seek to control information media, the press, radio and television. To try to deprive the various political parties or those who wish to express their views in public of these publication and communication media would, in my opinion, be tantamount to depriving the citizens of a free country of the exercise of their freedom.
I think the hon. member himself would be the first to condemn the state, the Canadian government for instance, if a member of his party or himself were to be prevented tomorrow from expressing their views and their policies to the citizens of the province of Quebec or of Canada, as they have done so freely since 1962 and during the previous years.
However, I will admit with the hon. member that liberty does not mean licence and that those are two entirely different things.
I believe that when public order and morals are seriously threatened, something should be done so that, as I said before, we may not be crushed under the dictatorship of a totalitarian government. We want our government to remain democratic and if the ideas spread by state broadcasting tended to upset the established order, I believe that some action would be necessary.
However, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-since, I presume, we want to single out the C.B.C.-is independent of the Canadian government, and belongs to all the taxpayers and the Canadian population. When the corporation was established, directors were appointed, and I believe that, to prevent it from being controlled by the state, its officials can intervene when it seems that certain limits have been exceeded.
